source.title: Less can be more for predicting properties with large language models
source.authors: Nawaf Alampara; Santiago Miret; K. Jablonka

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether scaling predicts downstream performance in materials-property tasks, using RMSE rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy or fitted language-model scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study tests dataset-size and model-size scaling for downstream materials-property prediction, but does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit power laws, extrapolate from small runs, or find a compute-optimal parameter/token split. Its representation, tokenizer, n-gram, and external benchmark results do not test the listed scaling-law versions.
record.test_reason: The study asks whether scaling pretraining data (BERT, 30K to 2M crystal structures) or model size (Llama-2 7B/13B/70B, LoRA) improves downstream materials-property RMSE. This is a new setting (crystal-structure text, regression targets) with a direct result on V6. It does not fit power laws, measure pretraining loss, or extrapolate, so it is T3 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that LLMs fail to use coordinate (geometric) information in coordinate-category data and behave like n-gram models. This persists across representations, tokenizers, dataset size (up to 2M structures) and model size (up to 70B), with scaling giving no meaningful gains. GNNs consistently outperform LLMs on these tasks (the 'GNN-LM wall').
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates downstream materials-property RMSE after pretraining or finetuning, rather than held-out language-model pretraining loss; it does not fit scaling laws or test compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: For Llama finetuning, the authors report that smaller warmup ratios caused more invalid generations; rank and learning-rate changes showed no significant performance difference within five-fold cross-validation error bars.
record.problems: The study reports downstream property-prediction results rather than pretraining loss. Scaling outcomes are presented graphically by representation and property, while the text gives only the aggregate statement of no effect; individual plotted values are not stated in the text. The authors also note that comprehensive hyperparameter optimization was infeasible.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 6 shows separate scaling curves by representation and property, but the supplied text does not give their individual values; the aggregate findings stated in the text are recorded in r1 and r2. Tokenizer comparisons and representation comparisons were not included because they do not test the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss is reported or fitted against parameters, tokens or compute.
No fits on small runs and no extrapolation.
No depth/width or shape variation at fixed parameter count.
Crystal-text pretraining and finetuning are other regimes, but no power-law form is fitted, so whether the same functional form holds is untested.
No fitted exponents or fitting choices are examined.
Predictability of downstream performance from pretraining loss is untested. Natural-language downstream tasks are not studied.

record.verdict_notes: The scaling result is a side ablation in a paper about geometric blindness. The evidence is coarse: 4 data points and 3 model sizes, five-fold cross-validation, and results shown only graphically (Figure 6) with a single aggregate textual statement. The model-scaling arm uses quantized LoRA finetuning of fixed checkpoints, and hyperparameter optimization was limited, so the absent effect may partly reflect the finetuning setup. The 'challenges' verdicts apply only to this materials-property setting.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their trends with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Whether power-law forms hold in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests dataset/model scaling for selected materials-property tasks, but not downstream predictability from pretraining loss or other downstream task families.
Fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.

rows.baseline: Mean RMSE with the 30,000-structure dataset for that representation
rows.value: The authors report no effect of dataset-size scaling on the investigated representations and prediction targets.
rows.uncertainty: Five-fold cross-validation; Figure 6 shading spans the minimum to maximum RMSE percentage changes across individual folds. Exact values are not stated in the text.
rows.note: Aggregate result stated for all investigated representations and prediction targets; Figure 6 displays separate curves, but their individual values are not provided in the text.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. Only four dataset sizes were tested. BERT is pretrained on crystal-structure text, not natural language. Per-representation values exist only in Figure 6. The baseline is the 30K mean RMSE per representation.

relationships.condition: BERT pretrained from scratch on 30K to 2M crystal-structure text samples, finetuned on shear modulus, bulk modulus and perovskite formation energy
relationships.reason: r1: authors state no effect of dataset scaling on RMSE for any representation or target; changes fall within fold-variation band.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing BERT pretraining data produced no detectable RMSE improvement for any representation or target, with changes within variation across folds.

relationships.condition: Llama-2 7B, 13B and 70B, 4-bit LoRA finetuned on the same three materials-property targets
relationships.reason: r2: authors state no effect of parameter-count scaling on RMSE; changes fall within fold-variation band.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing Llama-2 size produced no detectable RMSE improvement, with changes within variation across folds.
